title: Col. James Smith, captive, scout and Cane Ridge elder
summary: Taken captive at 18 in 1755, James Smith learned the woods as an adopted Mohawk, walked the Tennessee country in 1766, and settled near Cane Ridge in 1788.
bodyMarkdown:
In the summer of 1755, eighteen-year-old James Smith was helping cut a wagon road west from Fort Loudon, Pennsylvania, to join [General Braddock’s road](https://grokipedia.com/page/Braddock_Expedition) when a war party took him captive. He ran the gauntlet, was [adopted into a Kahnawake Mohawk family](https://history.ky.gov/kentucky-ancestors/colonel-james-smiths-death-verified), and learned their languages, hunting, and way of war. When he [escaped in 1759](https://www.heinzhistorycenter.org/blog/fort-pitt-museum/portrait-of-a-frontiersman-james-smith) and walked home, his own family did not know him at first.

What he had learned shaped the rest of his life. During [Pontiac’s War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Pontiac%27s_War) he dressed a ranger company, the “Black Boys,” in breechcloths and war paint, and in 1765 they [stopped a packhorse train](https://www.heinzhistorycenter.org/blog/fort-pitt-museum/portrait-of-a-frontiersman-james-smith) carrying “warlike stores” to the Ohio Indian trade.

## Eleven months in the wilderness

In late June 1766 Smith set out to see the country west of the mountains for himself. As [he told it in his own narrative](https://archive.org/details/accountofremarka00smit), he went west from the Holston River with Joshua Horton, Uriah Stone, William Baker, another James Smith, and an enslaved youth of about eighteen named Jamie whom Horton had brought along. They explored the country south of Kentucky and followed the Cumberland and [Tennessee rivers](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tennessee_River) to the Ohio; the stream they named for Uriah Stone is still Stones River.

At the mouth of the Tennessee, where [Paducah](https://grokipedia.com/page/Paducah,_Kentucky) stands now, the others went on toward the Illinois country. Smith turned for home, and Horton lent him Jamie. About eight days east, a sharp cane stalk drove into Smith’s foot and the leg swelled. With a knife and a moccasin awl he cut around the splinter while Jamie pulled it out with a pair of bullet molds. Jamie built a shelter thatched with cane tops, and the two lived on jerked buffalo while the foot healed. For three months, Smith wrote, he saw no other human being.

They reached the Carolina settlements in October. Settlers did not believe anyone had walked from the mouth of the Tennessee, or that a man would lend his slave for such a trip, and held Smith under guard until an old acquaintance vouched for him. He left Jamie at Horton’s quarter as he had promised. Smith’s book is the only record of Jamie, and nothing in Jamie’s own words survives.

## Cane Ridge

Smith served as a militia colonel in the Revolution, and in 1788 he brought his second wife, Margaret Rodgers Irvin, and their families to [Bourbon County](https://grokipedia.com/page/Bourbon_County,_Kentucky). He [bought 100 acres from James Garrard](https://history.ky.gov/kentucky-ancestors/colonel-james-smiths-death-verified) near Cane Ridge, about eight miles east of Paris, sat in the Danville convention on separation from Virginia, and served in the 1799 constitutional convention and the General Assembly. He was an elder of the church at the [Cane Ridge Meeting House](/stories/cane-ridge-meeting-house-and-the-1801-camp-meeting/).

In 1799 John Bradford printed Smith’s captivity narrative in Lexington. About then he sat for [an unknown Kentucky painter](https://www.heinzhistorycenter.org/blog/fort-pitt-museum/portrait-of-a-frontiersman-james-smith) in a fringed hunting shirt and a red handkerchief. Later he preached as a Presbyterian missionary among Ohio Valley Indians, published two attacks on the [Shakers](https://grokipedia.com/page/Shakers) after his son joined them, and in 1812 wrote a treatise on Indian warfare.

At seventy-four he followed the army to Fort Wayne. On his way back he fell ill at a nephew’s home in Green County and [died April 11, 1813](https://history.ky.gov/kentucky-ancestors/colonel-james-smiths-death-verified). His grave has never been found.

The map pin marks the Cane Ridge Meeting House, where Smith was an elder. His own farm nearby is not mapped.
Source: [Kentucky Historical Society: Colonel James Smith’s Death Verified](https://history.ky.gov/kentucky-ancestors/colonel-james-smiths-death-verified)
